name: The Law of Demeter
aliases: Only talk to your immediate friends
statement: Each unit should talk only to its immediate friends, and never to strangers.
meaning: A method should call methods on things it already knows about — itself, what it was handed, what it holds, what it just made — and not go reaching through those things to get at their internals. Reaching further means knowing the shape of somebody else's structure, and that knowledge becomes a dependency on it.
mechanism: Formally, a method may invoke methods only on: itself, its own parameters, objects it creates, its own attributes, and accessible globals. The practical shorthand is 'use only one dot': a chain like a.getB().getC().doThing() states, in code, that the caller knows the internal structure of A and of B. It is now coupled to two designs it does not own, and either one changing shape breaks it — a break at a distance, in a file whose author never heard of it. Keeping calls one hop away limits how far a structural change can travel.

examples.tag: The chain that breaks at a distance
examples.text: order.getCustomer().getAddress().getPostcode() ties the caller to the internals of Order, Customer and Address. Changing how an address is stored breaks code three types away.
The teaching example: a paperboy who reaches into the customer's pocket, takes the wallet and removes the money. Correct in outcome, wrong in structure — the customer should be asked to pay.
Instead of pulling a value out to make a decision about it, send the decision inward: order.chargeTo(paymentMethod) rather than reading the balance and comparing it outside.

whyItMatters: It converts an abstract worry about coupling into a rule you can apply while reading a single line, which is rare and valuable. It is also the clearest statement of why encapsulation is not about making fields private: a getter that returns an object you then reach into has exposed the structure just as thoroughly as a public field would.

working.lead: Count the dots, then ask why
working.text: the count is a smell rather than a verdict. Two dots on a fluent builder or a stream pipeline are fine; two dots that walk somebody else's object graph are the case the rule is about.

working.lead: Move the behaviour to the data
working.text: if you keep fetching three things from an object to compute something, the computation probably belongs on that object.
the rule protects behaviour, not records. A plain data object with no logic has no internals to hide, and applying the rule to it just adds wrappers.

limits: The standard criticism is the cost of obeying it: propagating calls through wrappers takes time and space at runtime, and done poorly it inflates a class's interface with auxiliary methods that exist only to forward. That is a genuine trade — maintainability bought with complexity and some efficiency. It also does not apply cleanly to data-transfer objects, to fluent interfaces, or to standard-library types whose structure is stable by contract, and mechanical enforcement by counting dots produces false positives in all three.
misreadings: It is not a law in any sense stronger than a design guideline, and the name is a project name, not a claim to lawfulness. It is not a rule against method chaining as such. And 'don't talk to strangers' does not forbid using objects you were given — those are friends; strangers are the objects you reach through them to find.
origin: Proposed by Ian Holland at Northeastern University in late 1987, during work on the Demeter Project — an adaptive-programming research effort named after the Greek goddess of agriculture, chosen to signal a bottom-up philosophy of programming and as a sister name to Zeus, the project's hardware description language. So the law is named after a goddess by way of a research project, not after a person who stated it.

sources.text: "Law of Demeter." Wikipedia — Ian Holland's authorship at Northeastern in 1987, the Demeter Project naming, the formal statement of which methods may be called, and the documented criticisms.
Lieberherr, K. & Holland, I. (1989). "Assuring Good Style for Object-Oriented Programs." IEEE Software 6(5). — the law as published by the Demeter group.
